chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, all from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ismail al-Basri, from Fuzayl ibn Yasar, who said:

I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'A number of Muslims went out on a journey, and they lost the way, so intense thirst struck them. They enshrouded themselves and stayed by the bases of the trees. Then an old man came to them, wearing white clothes, and said,
Arise, for there is no harm upon you, for this is water.

So they arose, drank, and were quenched. They said, 'Who are you? May Allah have mercy on you.' He said, 'I am from the Jinn who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). I heard the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) say: The believer is the brother of the believer, his eye, and his guide. Thus, you did not become wasted in my presence.'
ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the believer being described as the 'eye and guide' of another believer in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) illustrates the cosmic dimension of *al-ukhuwwah* (brotherhood), where a Jinn, having pledged allegiance to the Prophet, acts as a divine agent of care for humans based on their mutual bonds. The narrative highlights that the spiritual status of a believer extends beyond the human realm, influencing the natural world and serving as a practical mandate for vigilance and support among the faithful. It underscores the Shia understanding that adherence to prophetic teachings creates a tangible network of protection and guidance that transcends physical presence.
